grades.requirement:
Start with authoritative U.S. sources:

https://www.fda.gov/drugs
https://www.fda.gov/drugs/information-consumers-and-patients-drugs/find-information-about-drug
https://medlineplus.gov/medicines.html
https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/daf/

FDA's Drugs@FDA contains information on FDA-approved prescription and OTC human drugs, while MedlinePlus provides patient-oriented medication information from the National Library of Medicine.

Identify the major OTC pain/fever medicine categories relevant to a general U.S. consumer, including at minimum:

Acetaminophen
Ibuprofen
Naproxen
Aspirin

Do not assume that all products containing these ingredients are interchangeable.

Create an initial medication inventory containing:

Active Ingredient	Common U.S. Brand Examples	Drug Class	OTC Status	Primary Uses

Use the active ingredient, not merely the brand name, as the primary identifier.
grades.reasoning: The agent conducted various searches related to the task but failed to create the requested "initial medication inventory" containing Active Ingredient, Common U.S. Brand Examples, Drug Class, OTC Status, and Primary Uses as a structured guide/table. While it gathered bits of information, it did not fulfill the specific structural requirement of the rubric to compile this inventory.

grades.requirement:
For each active ingredient, locate current U.S. labeling through FDA and/or DailyMed.

For each medicine:

Search the active ingredient.
Open relevant current labeling.
Identify the dosage forms covered.
Determine whether multiple formulations exist.
Record important differences between formulations.
Record the label's intended uses.
Record warnings and precautions.
Record directions for use.
Record age-related restrictions or instructions.
Save the direct source URL.

Do not rely on an old blog post or retailer description when the official label is available.

FDA notes that DailyMed provides current marketed-drug labeling, while Drugs@FDA provides FDA-approved labeling and regulatory information; these sources can sometimes differ in update timing.
grades.reasoning:
The agent failed to fulfill the core requirements of the rubric. The rubric specifically requires the agent to search for the active ingredient, open current labeling from FDA/DailyMed, and then extract specific details (dosage forms, multiple formulations, intended uses, warnings, directions, age-related restrictions) and record the direct source URL for *each* medicine. 

The trajectory shows the agent performed Google searches for high-level safety information and retail pricing, but it never navigated to the FDA DailyMed or Drugs@FDA websites to open specific product labels. Consequently, the agent did not extract or record the required labeling information (dosage, warnings, uses, etc.) or save the direct source URLs for those labels as instructed.

For every active ingredient, document:

Pain relief

Common conditions for which consumers may encounter the medicine

Whether the information comes from labeling or general patient education

FDA/label-supported uses

from

General medical information

However, the agent's action history shows it spent almost the entire time searching for recall data and pricing at retail stores. The rubric required documenting specific details for *each* active ingredient regarding pain relief, fever reduction, inflammation-related uses, common conditions, whether use is included in OTC labeling, and whether the information comes from labeling or general education, while also separating these sources. The agent did not navigate to MedlinePlus, nor did it perform the systematic extraction and documentation of these specific required fields for each ingredient (acetaminophen, ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin). The actions were primarily focused on finding pricing and recall news, failing to satisfy the analytical requirements of the rubric.

Specifically, the rubric requires the agent to "open the official label and identify the most important warnings" for each of the major over-the-counter medicines (acetaminophen, ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin), separating them into "common side effects," "serious or medically important adverse effects," and "situations where the medicine may be inappropriate or require professional guidance."

The actions were primarily focused on retail pricing, recall searches, and general safety information snippets, rather than systematically investigating and synthesizing the specific warnings listed on official medication labels as required by the prompt.
